To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the inhibition of virus production by means, of hygromycine B is correlated with the increasing plasma membrane permeabilization to the drug that occurs during infection.

(i) the plasma membrane of animal cells infected with animal viruses becomes leaky to certain translation inhibitors; (ii) this membrane alteration occurs at a time when viral protein synthesis is very active; and (iii) the presence of these translation inhibitors in the culture medium inhibits viral production.
the inhibition of viral protein synthesis by means of translation-inhibiting drugs unable to penetrate normal plasma membrane can significantly reduce virus production in infected cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the interaction between animal viruses and normal cells and the development of methods for the inhibition of viral replication in vivo.
the study of the mechanisms of action of antiviral agents, and with the elucidation of the mechanisms of viral protein synthesis and virus maturation in animal virus-infected cells.
the study of the molecular basis of viral pathogenesis and the development of new antiviral agents based on the inhibition of viral protein synthesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in the three systems investigated the membrane permeability to low molecular weight inhibitors increases during the infection, in parallel with the increase of viral protein synthesis, and this alteration of the membrane permeability is correlated with a reduced virus production.
the plasma membrane of animal cells is permeable to hygromyin B only after it is infected by animal viruses.
the membrane leakiness is a consequence of the viral infection and that it can be exploited to inhibit viral protein synthesis and, hence, virus maturation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inhibition of virus protein synthesis by hygromycine B in infected cells, which have lost their membrane permeability barrier, may be an effective antiviral strategy.

, in all three systems, the virus production is correlated with a leakiness of the cell membranes, which allows the passage of translation inhibitors unable, in normal cells, to penetrate the plasma membrane.
the plasma membrane of infected cells becomes leaky to low-molecular weight inhibitors of translation and that this alteration is a prerequisite for viral protein synthesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the membrane leakiness is a very early event in the viral infection cycle.
the membrane permeability to translation inhibitors is a useful parameter to monitor virus production.
the plasma membrane of animal virus-infected cells is leakier than the plasma membrane of uninfected cells and that the leakiness is correlated with the extent of viral protein synthesis.
